statement: In people of European descent and in Chinese men, genetic variants that predict more drinking, compared with variants that predict less, are associated with more coronary heart disease in the European studies but not with heart attacks in the Chinese study; in its main analysis none of the four genetic studies read found lower coronary risk with genetically higher intake, none can show the shape of the curve at low intake with confidence, and a published critique argues that such studies remain observational and have biases of their own. No study gives absolute risks. In 56 European-descent studies (261,991 people), carriers of a variant of the alcohol-metabolising gene ADH1B reported 17.2% less drinking (95% CI 15.6% to 18.9%) and had lower odds of coronary heart disease (odds ratio 0.90, 0.84 to 0.96; 20,259 events); the authors had predicted that a protective effect of light to moderate drinking would show as higher odds in carriers who drank lightly to moderately, but the odds were similar at every level of drinking and each of those estimates was compatible with no difference (more than 0 to under 7 UK units of 7.9 g a week, 0.90, 0.79 to 1.02), and the variant went with lower blood pressure even in people who said they did not drink (Holmes et al., 2014). In UK Biobank (371,463 people), a genetic score built from variants for alcohol use disorder was associated with coronary artery disease, odds ratio 1.38 (1.10 to 1.74) per standard deviation of genetically predicted intake (a unit the paper does not define), and curves fitted with a method whose key assumption was not tested rose from the first drink, though a second score suggested no rise below roughly 7 to 14 drinks of 14 g a week, with slight decreases at modest intake for hypertension and in some analyses in women (Biddinger et al., 2022). In European summary data with up to 94 variants, the odds ratio was 1.16 (1.00 to 1.36) per standard deviation of log drinks a week and 1.08 (0.91 to 1.27) after allowing for genetic liability to smoking, which the variants also predicted; the ADH1B variant alone was associated with coronary artery disease (Larsson et al., 2020). In 161,498 genotyped Chinese adults, men's genotype-predicted mean intakes (4 to 256 g a week by group) were not associated with heart attack (relative risk 0.96, 0.78 to 1.18, per 280 g a week, which is 40 g a day; 1,696 cases) or with coronary heart disease (1.05, 0.94 to 1.17), although self-reported drinking in the same men showed lower heart-attack rates at moderate intake than in non-drinkers (Millwood et al., 2019). Three epidemiologists (Mukamal, Stampfer & Rimm, 2020; no funding or interests statement printed) argue that such analyses can be biased by ancestry, by parents' genes and drinking, by weak links between genes and reported intake, by genes that act through acetaldehyde rather than amount, by lowering heavy drinking days together with average intake, and by testing lifelong rather than adult drinking; they quantify none of these and report no figures from the studies they criticize, and Roerecke and Rehm (2014) likewise set the ADH1B result aside because the variant also lowers binge drinking. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: Some people carry genes that make them drink less, or more. Comparing them avoids some of the problems of asking people how much they drink. In studies of people of European descent, genes for drinking less went with slightly less heart disease, and genes for drinking more with more. In a large study of Chinese men, genes for drinking more made no difference to heart attacks either way. None of these studies found that genes for drinking more lowered heart risk. One UK study suggested that risk rises from the first drink, but a different set of genes gave a different answer. Three researchers argue that gene studies can be misled, for example by family background, by heavy drinking days, or by genes that act in other ways; they did not measure how much this matters. None of the studies says how many people out of 100 are affected.
population: People of European descent in 56 pooled studies (Holmes et al.), in UK Biobank (Biddinger et al.) and in genome-wide consortia with UK Biobank (Larsson et al.); adults in ten areas of China (China Kadoorie Biobank; genetic coronary results for men, women as a check); and a published methodological critique
exposure: Genetically predicted alcohol intake: carriage of the ADH1B rs1229984 A-allele (lower intake); a 5-variant score for alcohol use disorder scaled to genetically predicted intake; up to 94 variants for log drinks a week; ALDH2 rs671 and ADH1B rs1229984 genotypes combined with area into six groups of mean male intake (4 to 256 g/week)
comparator: Non-carriers, or lower genetically predicted intake (per standard deviation; per 280 g/week of genotype-predicted mean male intake against the lowest group)
outcome: Coronary heart disease or coronary artery disease (incident and prevalent events in the ADH1B study), heart attack (myocardial infarction), and the shape of the association at low intake
magnitude: Holmes et al. 2014 (56 studies, 261,991 European-descent people; ADH1B rs1229984 A-allele carriers against non-carriers): weekly intake 17.2% lower (15.6% to 18.9%), binge drinking OR 0.78 (0.73–0.84), abstention 1.27 (1.21–1.34); coronary heart disease OR 0.90 (0.84–0.96; 20,259 events; I² 17%), 0.81 (0.72–0.91) in four studies with at least 1,000 events; self-reported non-drinkers 0.98 (0.88–1.10), drinkers 0.86 (0.78–0.94), difference P = 0.095; light (more than 0 to under 7 UK units/week of 7.9 g) 0.90 (0.79–1.02), moderate (7 to under 21) 0.89 (0.75–1.06), heavy (21 or more) 0.97 (0.76–1.24), trend P = 0.83; systolic blood pressure in self-reported non-drinkers −0.80 mm Hg (−1.41 to −0.19); no instrumental-variable estimate. Biddinger et al. 2022 (UK Biobank, 371,463; 5-variant score for alcohol use disorder, F 780; OR per SD of genetically predicted intake): coronary artery disease 1.38 (1.10–1.74; P = .006), myocardial infarction 1.37 (1.05–1.78; P = .02, above the paper's threshold of P < .008); nonlinear: quadratic fit best (P < .001), risk rising from zero intake with the primary score; secondary score: no rise until roughly 7 to 14 drinks (14 g) a week. Larsson et al. 2020 (up to 94 variants; per SD of log drinks/week): coronary artery disease 1.16 (1.00–1.36; P = 0.052), 1.08 (0.91–1.27) adjusted for genetic liability to smoking initiation; never-smokers 1.39 (0.98–1.96); instrument and smoking initiation OR 1.24 (1.15–1.33); ADH1B variant alone, positive (P < 0.05). Millwood et al. 2019 (China Kadoorie Biobank men; six genotype–area groups, mean intake 4 to 256 g/week; per 280 g/week, which is 40 g/day): myocardial infarction RR 0.96 (0.78–1.18; 1,696 cases), coronary heart disease 1.05 (0.94–1.17; 6,145 cases); single variants (GG against AG) myocardial infarction rs671 1.02 (0.92–1.13), rs1229984 1.11 (0.95–1.31); women 0.94 (0.74–1.20). Mukamal et al. 2020: no estimates. No absolute risks in any study.

evidence.extracted: An essay, with no methods, data or effect estimates of its own, arguing that Mendelian randomization is an instrumental-variable method subject to confounding, weak-instrument bias, pleiotropy, adaptation and failure of replication; that the example of alcohol and cardiovascular disease shows it must be treated with the caution due to all observational epidemiology; and that it should be renamed genetic instrumental variable analysis, without the words randomization or causality.

evidence.locator: Confounding, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (the 2nd begins on p. 2)
evidence.extracted: Population structure: the ADH1B variant used as an instrument in alcohol analyses (its refs 1 and 2, Holmes et al. and Millwood et al.) is said to be most common in people of East Asian and Middle-Eastern descent, including Jews; in the ADH1B analysis it went with lower reported drinking but also with more education, which the authors read as likely to reflect ancestry and a healthier lifestyle (no figures given). Adjustment with a few principal components succeeds only if the subpopulation is large enough to appear among them, and Ashkenazi Jews are about 0.2% of Europe's population. Parental genotype: carriers of variants that lower drinking carry them from at least one parent and so are less likely to have been raised by a parent with alcohol dependence, which the essay cites as a risk factor for later cardiovascular disease.

evidence.locator: Weak instrument bias, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Pleiotropy, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The essay says genetic analyses should always report how strongly the instrument is associated with intake and that self-reported drinking is misreported in both directions; it infers likely weak-instrument bias and pleiotropy in the ADH1B analysis from the genotype's null association with HDL cholesterol, which alcohol raises in trials, without reporting that analysis's genotype–intake association. It argues that the ALDH2 variant raises acetaldehyde exposure in people who drink and so may affect risk directly, and that the stronger genetic associations in people who drank than in people who did not, in the ADH1B analysis, may reflect greater toxicity when alcohol is drunk rather than lower intake.

Drinking has at least three dimensions (frequency, usual quantity per occasion, binge drinking) that correlate only partly and differ in their cardiovascular effects; genetic variants lower all three, so genetic analyses cannot separate them, and those linking intake-lowering variants to lower cardiovascular risk may be showing the harm of binge drinking. Genotype tests lifelong (and parental) rather than adult exposure; given common heavy drinking in adolescence and early adulthood, its lower prevalence in young adults carrying ALDH2 variants, and the possibility that binge drinking starts atherosclerosis (a mouse study and a vascular-function study are cited), such analyses may partly test teenage and young-adult heavy drinking, with uncertain relevance to limited drinking in mid-life.

evidence.locator: Interpreting inconsistency; An appropriate role for GIVA; Summary; Acknowledgements (p. 4); References 17 to 19 (p. 5)
evidence.extracted: The essay says genetic analyses are not immune from inconsistent results and selective publication, and sets the Chinese analysis (its ref. 2), which it says combined genetic and ecological instruments and claimed dose-dependent harm for stroke with no effect on heart attack, against three East Asian reports of higher coronary risk with the ALDH2 variant, which by their titles are a genome-wide association study, an exome-chip meta-analysis and a meta-analysis of gene variants, not instrumental-variable analyses of alcohol. It offers folate and the MTHFR gene as a case in which genetic findings agreed with trials once intake was known, a model it says does not extend easily to alcohol, and concludes that the approach is fundamentally observational. The PDF prints 'Acknowledgements None' and no funding or conflict-of-interest statement.

risk_of_bias.note: The genetic design protects against confounding by lifestyle and against illness changing drinking, because genotype is fixed at conception (the cards rate confounding some concerns, not high), so the editors do not rate down for classical confounding. It does not protect against pleiotropy (the European instrument predicted smoking initiation, and its coronary estimate fell from 1.16 to 1.08 after allowing for it; the ADH1B variant went with lower blood pressure, interleukin-6 and body mass index in people reporting no drinking; scores for alcohol use disorder may act on other behaviours), selection (studies joined by collaboration and prevalent cases in the ADH1B study; UK Biobank volunteers; estimates within strata of reported drinking, which genotype itself changes) or sample overlap (UK Biobank in both exposure and outcome data). Weak instruments are not the problem here (F 780 in UK Biobank; more than 50-fold differences in mean intake in China). Because the pleiotropy checks moved one estimate to no difference, rated down one level.

inconsistency.note: The European studies point to more coronary disease with genetically higher intake (0.90 for the intake-lowering variant; 1.16 to 1.38 per SD); the Chinese study, with the largest genetic differences in intake, finds no association with heart attack (0.96) or coronary heart disease (1.05). Not explained by the sources (ancestry, mainly spirits in China, different genes, different outcome definitions).

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: what the genetic studies find. As evidence about light drinking in adult life it would be indirect (genotypes mark lifelong differences; the European estimates are per SD of genetically predicted intake and cannot be put into grams; only one analysis addresses low intake, with an untested assumption); stated rather than rated, as certainty is already at the floor.

imprecision.note: The Chinese heart-attack estimate (0.78 to 1.18; 1,696 cases) includes both a fifth lower and a fifth higher risk; the European summary-data estimate is borderline (1.00 to 1.36); the ADH1B drinking-category estimates each include no difference.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable with four studies; the ADH1B study used mainly unpublished genetic data.

grade.reasoning: Mendelian randomization is observational and starts low (round brief). The genetic design addresses confounding by lifestyle and reverse causation, which is why risk of bias is rated down for pleiotropy, selection and sample overlap rather than for classical confounding; those threats, and the inability to show a curve at low intake (the one nonlinear analysis changed with the score used), remain. Rated down for risk of bias, inconsistency and imprecision, which is below the floor: very low. Rated as worded: genetic associations; whether they show that alcohol raises, or does not lower, coronary risk is the question of the debate box. Not fully independent: Holmes et al. and Millwood et al. share two authors, and Larsson et al. and Biddinger et al. both use UK Biobank outcome data. The critique (Mukamal et al.) concerns Holmes et al. and Millwood et al. only and was published before the other two. Status contested: credible results point in different directions and a published critique changes how they are read.

debate.question: Do the gene studies show that drinking more raises the risk of heart disease, and that a little drinking does not protect the heart?
debate.evidence_yes: The genetic design avoids the two biases that critics of cohort studies stress most: genotype is fixed at conception, so it is not chosen together with a lifestyle, and it is not changed by illness, as drinking can be. With strong instruments, three European-descent analyses point the same way: carriers of the ADH1B variant, who reported 17% less drinking, had lower odds of coronary heart disease (0.90, 0.84 to 0.96; 0.81 in the four largest studies), and the pattern the authors had said a protective effect would produce, higher odds in carriers who drank lightly or moderately, did not appear (Holmes et al., 2014; sc_holmes_2014); a score for alcohol use disorder (F statistic 780) gave 1.38 (1.10 to 1.74) per SD in UK Biobank, with three methods robust to some pleiotropy pointing the same way and no association with the outcomes in 34,423 lifelong abstainers apart from HDL cholesterol and apolipoprotein A (Biddinger et al., 2022; sc_biddinger_2022); and up to 94 variants gave 1.16 (1.00 to 1.36), larger in never-smokers (1.39, 0.98 to 1.96), with the ADH1B variant alone also positive (Larsson et al., 2020; sc_larsson_2020). In Chinese men the dip in heart attacks seen with self-reported drinking did not appear when men were grouped by genotype (Millwood et al., 2019; sc_millwood_2019): in its main analysis, no genetic study read found lower coronary risk with genetically higher intake.
debate.evidence_no: The genetic results are not consistent and rest on assumptions that cannot all be checked. With the strongest instrument, in Chinese men, genetically higher intake showed no association with heart attack (0.96, 0.78 to 1.18) or coronary heart disease (1.05, 0.94 to 1.17), neither harm nor benefit (Millwood et al., 2019). In European summary data the coronary association was borderline and fell to 1.08 (0.91 to 1.27) after allowing for genetic liability to smoking, which the alcohol variants also predicted (odds ratio 1.24 for starting to smoke) (Larsson et al., 2020). The ADH1B variant went with lower blood pressure, interleukin-6 and body mass index in people who reported not drinking, about as much as in people who drank lightly, which points either to misreported drinking or to a path other than alcohol; its light-drinking estimate (0.90, 0.79 to 1.02) is compatible with no difference; and carriers had slightly more education (Holmes et al., 2014). The UK Biobank curves that rise from the first drink come from a method that is valid only if the score shifts intake by the same amount at every level, which was not tested, and a second score gave no rise below roughly 7 to 14 drinks a week, with slight decreases at modest intake for hypertension and in some analyses in women, which the authors attribute to pleiotropy in that score (Biddinger et al., 2022). A published critique (Mukamal et al., 2020; sc_mukamal_2020) argues that the ADH1B variant is most common in people of East Asian and Middle-Eastern descent, so ancestry could confound it in European data (Ashkenazi Jews are about 0.2% of Europe's population, too few for standard ancestry adjustment to capture); that parents' genes shape exposure to a parent's alcohol dependence in childhood; that the variant's null association with HDL cholesterol, which alcohol raises in trials, suggests a weak instrument; that ALDH2 variants raise acetaldehyde in people who drink, so stronger associations in people who drink may reflect toxicity rather than amount; that genes lower heavy drinking days together with average intake, so the studies may be showing the harm of heavy drinking days; and that genotype tests lifelong, including youthful, drinking rather than limited drinking in mid-life. Roerecke and Rehm (2014; sc_roerecke_2014) also set the ADH1B result aside because the variant lowers binge drinking.
debate.neither_can_show: Neither side can show the shape of the curve at low intake with confidence: one variant or score shifts intake across the whole range, the European estimates are per SD of genetically predicted intake and cannot be put into grams, and the only nonlinear analysis depended on an untested assumption and on the score used. Genotypes mark lifelong differences in drinking, so the studies cannot separate adult from youthful drinking, or average amount from heavy drinking days. Whether the variants act only through the amount drunk cannot be proved: the critique shows that biases are possible but quantifies none, and the studies' checks (ancestry adjustment, people who do not drink as a negative control, pleiotropy-robust methods, allowance for smoking liability) reduce but cannot rule them out. The results come from people of European descent and from Chinese men; women in China served only as a check, because few drink. None of the studies reports absolute risks.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). The four genetic studies agree on one point: in its main analysis, none finds that genetically higher intake goes with lower coronary risk, which a real protective effect of drinking would predict. Beyond that they differ: the European studies find more coronary disease with genetically higher intake, though one estimate shrinks to no difference once genetic liability to smoking is allowed for, and the Chinese study, with the largest genetic differences in intake, finds neither more nor fewer heart attacks. The critique is right that these are observational analyses whose assumptions must be defended, and some of its concerns have support in the studies' own data (associations in people who say they do not drink; heavy drinking days moving with average intake); but it quantifies none of them, and the biases it names for genetic studies (confounding, misreported drinking, selective publication) apply equally to the cohort studies that show the protective association, which it does not discuss. Read together, the genetic evidence weakens the case that light drinking protects the heart, without showing that light drinking harms it or how large any effect at low intake might be.
debate.what_would_settle_it: Genetic analyses of new coronary events in several ancestries, including east Asian cohorts with many more heart attacks, using several independent alcohol variants, within-family designs to remove effects of ancestry and of parents, nonlinear methods that do not divide people by how much they say they drink, and people confirmed by biomarkers not to drink as a test of paths outside alcohol; reported with the strength of each instrument and with absolute risks. A long-term randomized trial of light drinking against not drinking would answer the light-drinking question directly. None of the sources read reports these.
